# The commentary of `ada83.c`

Every comment in the compiler, arranged to be read rather than to be
archived. Regenerate with `python3 tools/commentary.py`.

| | |
|---|---:|
| source lines | 62,830 |
| comments | 2,097 |
| design notes — Part I | 945 |
| short notes — Part III | 1,077 |
| section headings, listed only below | 71 |
| front matter | 1 |
| rules and boxes with no prose | 3 |
| clauses of the RM cited | 153 |

Every comment is accounted for: 945 + 1,077 + 71 + 1 + 3 = 2,097.

## How to read this

**Part I, the design notes**, is the part worth reading. Every comment of
four lines or more, under the declaration it introduces, gathered under
the section of the file it lives in.
These are the arguments — why a rule is where it is, which sentence of
the reference manual decides a case, what a field may not be used for.

**Part II, the RM index**, inverts the file: every clause of
ANSI/MIL-STD-1815A the source cites, and each place that cites it. This
is the part to reach for when changing a rule. A clause with several
entries is either one rule written in several places — which this
codebase treats as a defect in itself, since copies drift apart — or a
rule and its exceptions.

**Part III, the short notes**, is everything else, under the function it
sits in: the one- and two-line remarks that explain a line rather than a
decision.

Comments that are only a rule or a box are counted above and not
reproduced; the file banner is under *Front matter*, and the section
headings are listed on their own below.

## The nineteen sections

`ada83.c` is nineteen numbered sections, each opened by a banner in
the specification half and again in the body half. The banners are
boundaries, not signposts: everything between one and the next belongs
to the section it names, which is how Part I below is arranged. §13
is opened three times — once for the code generator's own state, once
for each of its numbered sub-sections, and once more for the
generators that follow them.

## Front matter

```
===================================================================
ada83 — an Ada 83 (ANSI/MIL-STD-1815A) compiler emitting LLVM IR.

One translation unit in nineteen sections.  Each has a specification
half — its types and its forward declarations — and a body half,
both carrying the same § number, and each half opens with a banner
that names the section, so a § below is a place the file can be
opened at.  A section's types are its vocabulary: read them and you
know what that part of the compiler is able to say.

  §1  Foundation      widths, the two 128-bit integers, target facts
  §2  Measurement     bits and bytes; LLVM_Rep, LLVM_Value, LLVM_I1
  §3  Memory          one bump arena; nothing is freed until exit
  §4  Text            non-owning String_Slice; case-folded hashing
  §5  Provenance      Source_Location and the diagnostic accumulator
  §6  Arithmetic      Big_Integer, Big_Real, Rational.  Ada's
                      universal types need exact arithmetic, and
                      IEEE doubles are not enough
  §7  Lexer           Token_Kind, Token, Lexer
  §8  Syntax          Node_Kind and the tree, pinned by
                      Syntax_Tree_Shape
  §9  Parser          recursive descent over the whole grammar
  §10 Types           Type_Info: the lattice, and also the
                      constraint, the view and the representation
  §11 Names           Symbol, Scope, Interpretation; two-phase
                      overload resolution
  §12 Semantics       name resolution, type checking, folding, and
                      the legality rules over the resolved tree
  §13 Code generation LLVM IR emission.  §13 opens with the code
                      generator's own state, the five numbered
                      sub-sections follow in order, and the
                      generators themselves close the section under
                      a second §13 banner:
    §13.1  primitives      the operand and value forms
    §13.2  runtime checks  Check_Kind, Check_Predicate, RM 11.7
    §13.3  fat pointers    {ptr, ptr} for unconstrained arrays
    §13.5  exceptions      handler frames and setjmp regions
    §13.10 build in place  BIP_*
  §14 Library         ALI files, checksums, dependency tracking
  §15 Elaboration     the unit graph and its topological order
  §16 Generics        macro-style instantiation: cloning a template,
                      binding its formals to actuals, remapping the
                      symbols of the copy.  The legality of a
                      generic declaration read on its own is §12's;
                      everything whose subject is an instance is
                      here
  §17 File loading    include-path search; circular-with detection
  §18 SIMD            compile-time dispatch, runtime feature detect
  §19 Driver          arguments; a worker process per input file

Four sections define a handful of functions in their specification
half rather than in their body — §1's and §2's measurements, §7's
readers of a character and of an operator symbol, and §10's
representation-aspect bit.  Each is total and one expression long,
and belongs to the vocabulary rather than to an algorithm over it.

One thing this vocabulary does not yet name, and one that it now
does.  Both are argued in ARCHITECTURE.md.

A subtype is a type together with a constraint (RM 3.3.2), and a
representation clause does not change the type (RM 13.1).  Neither
the constraint nor the representation is a type here: both live in
Type_Info's fields, so every use site separates them again by hand,
and a predicate about the language sits beside one about the ABI.

Between §12 and §13 sits the LOWERED FORM: what resolution
concluded, in the shape code generation consumes without asking the
syntax tree again.  Aggregate_Descriptor, Object_Shape,
Actual_Binding, Assignment_Destination, Element_Interval,
Storage_Locus and Generic_Actual_Binding are its vocabulary; five of
them are built and read inside §13 and can only be wrong, never
missing.  The part of the phase that is written on a node by §12 and
read off it by §13 is named once, in Lowering_Table (§8), which is
what lets a fill point be total and stops a clone inheriting a
conclusion drawn about the tree it was copied from.
===================================================================
```

## §5  Provenance

| | |
|---|---|
| `7418` | [Report_Driver_Error](#report-driver-error-7418) |

### Report_Driver_Error

```c
void Report_Driver_Error (const char *format, ...)
```

> A diagnostic about the compilation as a whole rather than about a
> position in a source file: an input that cannot be read, an option
> that is not recognised, a program with no consistent elaboration
> order.  There is no position to name, so the tool names itself.  The
> message is not gated on Diagnostics_Suppressed — that gate exists for
> speculative resolution, and none of these are speculative — but the
> error does count, which is how the driver's exit status learns about
> it.

`ada83.c:7418`

## §6  Arithmetic

| | |
|---|---|
| `360` | [typedef struct Machine_Format](#typedef-struct-machine-format-360) |

### typedef struct Machine_Format

> RM 13.7.3: a target floating point format, as the MACHINE_
> attributes describe it.  A machine number of the format is
> mantissa * RADIX**exponent, where mantissa has MANTISSA radix digits
> after the point and EXPONENT_MINIMUM <= exponent <= EXPONENT_MAXIMUM
> (RM 3.5.7's canonical form).  DECIMAL_DIGITS is the decimal
> precision the format sustains, which is the D of a type the
> implementation may back with it.

`ada83.c:360`

### typedef enum

> RM 4.5: the precedence of an infix operator.  Declared here rather
> than beside the parser because precedence is a property of the
> operator token — the table immediately below names one per token —
> and the parser is only its largest reader.

`ada83.c:440`

### typedef enum

> RM 2.9, RM 4.4, RM 4.5: what a token is, as a set of Token_Kind.  The
> primitive classes below are the RM's own groupings; the derived
> classes are unions of them, so a rule stated over "the relational
> operators" and a rule stated over "the equality operators" cannot
> drift apart.  Which token carries which class is stated once, in
> Token_Kind_Property_Table.

`ada83.c:449`

### TOKEN_CLASS_SHORT_CIRCUIT     = 1u << 6,

> RM 4.4: the binary forms that are written like operators and are
> not operators.  RM 6.7 turns on exactly this distinction —
> "neither membership tests nor the short-circuit control forms are
> allowed as function designators" — so it is a class and not a
> remark.

`ada83.c:467`

### TOKEN_CLASS_RECOVERY_ANCHOR   = 1u << 11,

> Not a rule of the language but of error recovery: the reserved
> words that open a declaration or a statement, and END, which
> closes one.  A parser that has abandoned a construct resumes at
> one of these, so a token either is a place to resume or is not.

`ada83.c:486`

### TOKEN_CLASS_ABOVE_SIMPLE_EXPRESSION = TOKEN_CLASS_LOGICAL |

> RM 4.4's grammar in one set.  An expression is built from relations
> by the logical operators and the short-circuit forms; a relation is
> built from simple expressions by the relational operators and the
> membership tests.  So a binary construct whose operator is in this
> class is NOT a simple expression, and — the same fact read the
> other way — its result is BOOLEAN.  Both readers ask this, and they
> used to ask it with two hand-written lists that had to agree.

`ada83.c:503`

### typedef enum

> RM 4.5.2: which outcomes of a comparison — the left operand below,
> equal to, or above the right — make a relational operator true.  The
> set IS the operator's definition, so a fold that has compared its
> operands exactly reads its answer here instead of re-deciding it.

`ada83.c:515`

### #define TOKEN_KIND_LIST(X) \

> RM 2.2: every token of Ada 83, with everything the compiler asks of
> one.  The columns after the class mask are stated only where they are
> not the default: a token that opens no expression has no precedence,
> a token that is not an operator of RM 4.5 has no operator symbol, and
> a token that is not a relational operator neither holds for any sign
> nor spells an LLVM comparison predicate.
> 
> SPELLING is how the token is named in a diagnostic.  For a reserved
> word that is also its lexeme, which is why Lookup_Keyword can read
> the column; for a token class it is the metaname ("identifier"), and
> for AND THEN and OR ELSE it is the two reserved words with the space
> the source may write between them.  OPERATOR_DESIGNATOR is a separate
> column because it is a separate thing: RM 6.7's operator_symbol, the
> characters between the quotation marks of a function designator.

`ada83.c:526`

### X (TK_NOT,       "NOT",       TOKEN_CLASS_RESERVED_WORD | TOKEN_CLASS_LOGICAL | \

> RM 4.5.1 gives NOT its unary logical reading and RM 4.5.2 its
> reading as the NOT of a negated membership test.  The token has
> both; which one applies is settled by where it is written, and the
> precedence column is the infix one.

`ada83.c:641`

### typedef struct

> RM 2.4: what one reading of a numeric literal's text yields - the base,
> the bounds of the numeral proper, how many of its digits fall after the
> point, and the exponent.  Everything that needs the literal's VALUE
> reads this instead of the text.
> 
> The literal's SHAPE - based or decimal, real or integer - is not here:
> those two facts steer the scan that fixes the literal's extent, so the
> scanner owns them.  Keeping them out means a literal that this walk
> rejects still carries the right token kind, and one lexical error does
> not become a shower of type errors.
> 
> EXPONENT_IS_NEGATIVE is kept beside the signed EXPONENT because RM 2.4.1
> forbids a written minus sign on an integer literal's exponent even when
> the exponent it introduces is zero.

`ada83.c:810`

### Token_From_Op_Name

```c
Token_Kind Token_From_Op_Name (String_Slice name)
```

> RM 6.7's operator_symbol read backwards: the token an operator symbol
> names, or TK_EOF for a sequence of characters that names none.  A row
> with no operator designator is a token that is not an operator of
> RM 4.5, and no such row can be reached by this scan.

`ada83.c:847`

### OPERATOR_SYMBOL_NOT_AN_OPERATOR,

> RM 6.7: "The sequence of characters of the operator symbol must be
> either a logical, a relational, a binary adding, a unary adding, a
> multiplying, or a highest precedence operator (see 4.5).  Neither
> membership tests nor the short-circuit control forms are allowed as
> function designators."  So "in", "not in", "and then", "or else" —
> and anything else that is not an operator at all, such as ":=" —
> name nothing that could be declared.  The token table gives the
> control forms no operator designator, so the lookup above never
> finds one.

`ada83.c:866`

### Operator_Admits_Parameter_Count

```c
bool Operator_Admits_Parameter_Count (Token_Kind op, uint32_t count)
```

> RM 6.7: "The subprogram specification of a unary operator must have a
> single parameter.  The subprogram specification of a binary operator
> must have two parameters", and "For each of the operators "+" and "-",
> overloading is allowed both as a unary and as a binary operator."
> 
> Which operators are unary is RM 4.5's classification, and the token
> table already carries it: UNARY_ONLY marks an operator that has only a
> unary form, ALSO_UNARY one that has both.  So the admissible counts
> are read off the table rather than listed again.

`ada83.c:891`

### typedef enum

> RM 6.7 names three ways a function whose designator is an operator
> symbol can be declared, and two of its rules turn on which one it is:
> the equality rule holds for a declaration "other than by a renaming
> declaration", and the ban on default expressions holds "whether the
> operator is declared with an explicit subprogram specification or by
> a generic instantiation".

`ada83.c:917`

### Scan_Identifier

```c
Token_Kind kind = TK_IDENTIFIER;
```

> RM 2.9: an identifier that spells one of the reserved words is that
> reserved word.  Which token kinds are reserved words is the token
> table's answer, so the scan no longer depends on them occupying one
> contiguous run of the enumeration — and AND THEN and OR ELSE, which
> are two reserved words apiece, are no longer compared against at all.
> The comparison is case-insensitive because RM 2.3 says the letters of
> an identifier may be written in either case.

`ada83.c:7958`

### Scan_Numeral

```c
void Scan_Numeral (Lexer *lex, bool extended_digits_allowed)
```

> RM 2.4.1/2.4.2: every numeral in a literal — the integer part, the
> fraction, the base, the based integer and the exponent — has the one
> shape  digit {[underline] digit} , with A .. F admitted as extended
> digits only between the delimiters of a based literal.  Scanning fixes
> the literal's extent only; whether the underscores really do separate
> two digits is settled by Decompose_Numeric_Literal.

`ada83.c:7994`

### Decompose_Numeric_Literal

```c
bool Decompose_Numeric_Literal (Source_Location location, String_Slice text,
```

> RM 2.4: a numeric literal is a chain of numerals joined by the
> punctuation  .  #  :  E  +  - , each of which may only ever stand
> BETWEEN two complete numerals.  The scanner has already fixed the
> literal's extent; this walk reads that text against the grammar,
> reports the first violation (the ACATS grader counts diagnostic lines,
> so one per malformed literal is exactly right), and keeps what it
> learns on the way — the base, the bounds of the numeral proper, how
> many of its digits fall after the point, and the exponent — so that
> nothing has to read the text a second time to find them again.
> 
> Regions: 0 = the decimal literal, or the base of a based one;
>          1 = between the based delimiters, where letters are digits;
>          2 = after the closing delimiter, where only an exponent may
>              follow.

`ada83.c:8029`

### Scan_Number

```c
Token Scan_Number (Lexer *lex)
```

> RM 2.4: scanning fixes the literal's shape — where it ends, whether a
> base delimiter opened it, and whether a point made it real.  Those two
> facts belong to the scan, because they are what steer it; the literal's
> VALUE belongs to Decompose_Numeric_Literal, which reads the text the
> scan delimited.  Keeping the two apart is what lets a literal the
> grammar walk rejects still carry the right token kind, so that one
> lexical error does not become a shower of type errors.

`ada83.c:8126`

### Scan_Number

```c
bool is_based = Lexer_Peek (lex, 0) == '#' or
```

> RM 2.4.2 with RM 2.10: a based literal opens with a sharp or, where
> that character is unavailable, with a colon, and must close with the
> same character it opened with.  Both ends conflict with other uses of
> the colon, and they are settled in opposite directions:
> 
> opening — a colon opens a based literal only when an extended digit
> follows it, so the colon of a ":=" cannot be mistaken for an opener;
> 
> closing — the closing colon is taken WHATEVER follows it.  The
> delimiter wins over the ":=" its own character might otherwise begin,
> which is what makes  0 .. 2:10::= 1  read as the literal 2:10: and
> then ":=".  Narrowing this to "not when '=' follows" is wrong and has
> been tried: it also breaks  3:10:=3:10: , where the closing colon is
> followed by an equality operator.

`ada83.c:8140`

### f

```c
if (Is_Alpha (Lexer_Peek (lex, 0)) or Lexer_Peek (lex, 0) == '_')
```

> RM 2.2: a numeric literal and an adjacent identifier, keyword or
> literal need a separator between them (1THEN, 16#D#_ ...).  A letter
> or an underscore right after the literal's last character can only be
> that mistake.

`ada83.c:8182`

### Scan_Number

```c
Big_Integer *magnitude;
```

> RM 2.4: the value of a numeral is its digits weighted by powers of
> the base.  One accumulation serves the decimal and the based forms;
> base ten takes the vectorised path, which wants the digits alone —
> the underscores carry no value, and neither does the point of a real
> literal, so the copy holds only what counts.  It is sized from the
> literal itself, so a numeral of any length is carried exactly.

`ada83.c:8191`

### typedef enum

> RM 9.7: the arms a select alternative can take.  RM 9.7.1 names the
> first three —
> 
>     selective_wait_alternative ::= accept_alternative
>        | delay_alternative | terminate_alternative
> 
> — and RM 9.7.2 / 9.7.3 add the entry call that opens a conditional or
> a timed entry call.  Which arm an alternative is decides both what it
> may be combined with and how it is executed, so the parser records it
> once rather than leaving later passes to guess from the shape of the
> statement it starts with.

### typedef enum

> RM 3.3, RM 3.5: the classes of types, as a set of Type_Kind.  The
> eleven primitive classes below partition the kinds; the derived
> classes are unions of them, so the containment laws of RM 3.5 — a
> discrete type is scalar, a numeric type is either integer or real —
> hold by construction instead of by several hand-written disjunctions
> agreeing with one another.  Which kinds carry which primitive class
> is stated once, in Type_Kind_Property_Table.
> 
> Declared here rather than beside Type_Info because RM Annex A's
> attribute table, immediately below, names a class per attribute.

`ada83.c:995`

### TYPE_CLASS_NONE           = 0,

> The empty class set.  It has two readings, and both are wanted:
> as the class set of a kind, "this kind is in no class at all";
> as an attribute's prefix class, "this attribute restricts nothing".
> Prefix_Class_Admits tests the mask for emptiness before it ever
> looks at a type, so the two never meet.

`ada83.c:1006`

### TYPE_CLASS_UNIVERSAL_INTEGER = 1u << 9,

> RM 4.10: the two anonymous types a literal has before its context
> converts it.  They are classes of their own because the questions
> the compiler asks of a universal type are not the questions it
> asks of the named type it will become.

`ada83.c:1024`

### TYPE_CLASS_SCALAR    = TYPE_CLASS_DISCRETE | TYPE_CLASS_REAL,

> RM 3.5: the scalar types are the discrete types together with the
> real types.  Both universal types are therefore scalar, and
> universal_integer is discrete (RM 3.5.4 makes it an integer type).
> 
> A universal type has no bound and no size to offer -- it reaches an
> object only through the implicit conversion of RM 4.10 -- so a
> caller that goes on to read a bound, size a slot, coerce a value or
> emit a check is not asking this question.  That caller asks
> TYPE_CLASS_SCALAR_REPRESENTATION, which is this class less the two
> universals.  The two questions were one predicate until the class
> table made the containment violation visible: Type_Is_Real was true
> of universal_real while Type_Has_Scalar_Representation was false, so the compiler
> had a real that was not a scalar.

`ada83.c:1041`

### typedef enum

> RM 4.1, Annex A: what an attribute's prefix is allowed to denote.
> Annex A states every attribute's prefix in one of three voices, and
> telling the three apart is the whole of the prefix rule:
> 
>   "denotes a <class> type or subtype"  -> TYPE_MARK
>   "denotes an object" -- also a component of a record object, an
>   entry, a program unit, a label                     -> OBJECT
>   "is appropriate for a <class> type"  -> APPROPRIATE
> 
> APPROPRIATE is the one voice that carries the implicit dereference of
> RM 4.1(4), and it carries it because RM 4.1(4) speaks of *the type
> of* the prefix -- which a type mark does not have.  So ACC'FIRST
> names the access type and is illegal (RM 3.6.2), while P'FIRST for an
> access object P reaches the array it designates.
> 
> An attribute with two Annex A entries names two voices; where the two
> entries also differ in the class they admit -- 'CONSTRAINED does --
> the table carries the union and the split is stated as its own rule.
> 
> Attributes outside Ada 83's Annex A are given ATTRIBUTE_PREFIX_ANY,
> which restricts nothing.

`ada83.c:1060`

### typedef enum

> What a written prefix turned out to denote.  Annex A's three voices
> above ask only "type mark or object"; RM 13.7.2 and RM 9.9 ask a
> finer question of the same prefix -- "for any object, program unit,
> label, or entry X", "for any component C of a record object R", "for
> a task object or value T" -- so the arms are the RM's own and the
> table below names the set each attribute admits.
> 
> The arms partition the prefixes: a name denotes exactly one of these
> things, and something that is not a name denotes a value.  UNRESOLVED
> is not an answer but the absence of one -- a prefix nothing was
> resolved for supports no rule, in either direction.  As with
> Type_Class_Mask, the empty set reads as "this attribute restricts
> nothing", which is what every Annex A entry that is silent about the
> kind of entity says.

`ada83.c:1090`

> Ada 83 defines 'VALUE for discrete prefixes only; the floating point

> decimal real literal with FLOAT'VALUE, so the extension is named
> here, admitted for floating point alone, and goes away the day
> rts/text_io.adb parses a decimal literal itself.

### Source_Location declarative_part_end;

> The token that closes this node's declarative part: its BEGIN, or
> its END when it has none.  RM 3.9 rules a declaration whose body is
> never given illegal at the point its declarative part closes, and
> RM 7.4.1 rules a private type whose full declaration is never given
> illegal at the END of the package specification; neither illegality
> is a property of any text inside the part, so neither has anywhere
> else to be reported.  A node that owns no declarative part closes
> where it begins, which keeps the field readable without a guard.

### typedef enum

> RM 3.3.2 names five forms of constraint.  The forms are bits because
> the honest answer to the question a type is asked -- which forms may
> constrain it -- is a set: a floating point type admits a range
> constraint (RM 3.5) and a floating accuracy constraint (RM 3.5.7); a
> fixed point type a range constraint and a fixed accuracy constraint
> (RM 3.5.9).  Asked of a constraint as written the answer is single,
> because RM 3.3.2 gives each form its own production and the parser
> gives each production its own node kind: the form is therefore a
> column of Node_Kind_Property_Table below, and Constraint_Node_Form
> reads it.

`ada83.c:1998`

### typedef enum

> RM 7.4.1 admits such a name in exactly one position and names three
> ways of not being in it.  The value is the verdict for the point the
> walk stands at; everything below that point inherits it, except that
> crossing a declaration decides it afresh — which is what gives the
> rule its "the declaration this occurrence is in" reading.
> 
> PRIVATE_NAME_POSITION_UNCHANGED is a table answer and never a carried
> verdict: a node kind that is not one of the declarations RM 7.4.1
> speaks about settles nothing, and the verdict in force stands.

`ada83.c:2019`

### typedef enum

> RM 7.4.3 admits the name of a deferred constant in exactly one place,
> "in the default expression for a record component or for a formal
> parameter (not for a generic formal parameter)".  The verdict is set
> on those two edges of the walk and on no other, and RM 4.4 leaves a
> default expression made of expressions alone, so nothing below one
> can take it back.

`ada83.c:2036`

### typedef uint32_t Node_Class_Mask;

> The classes of syntax, as a set of Node_Kind.  A question of the form
> "is a node of this kind one of these?" is a class, and every such
> question in the compiler is answered from Node_Kind_Property_Table
> and from nowhere else, so two of them can no longer disagree without
> the disagreement being written down in one place where it can be
> read.

`ada83.c:2053`

### NODE_CLASS_ENCLOSES_EXPRESSIONS     = 1u << 0,

> RM 4.4, RM 3.3.2: a construct all of whose constituents occur
> within an expression.
> 
> This is not the same question as "is this node an expression", and
> the difference is the whole reason the class exists.  A name is an
> expression (RM 4.4 makes a name a primary) and encloses none: RM
> 4.1 gives the prefix of an expanded name a declarative region to
> denote, not a value, and the selector denotes an entity.  A
> constraint is not an expression and encloses nothing else: RM 3.3.2
> writes every constraint out of simple expressions and discrete
> ranges.  A literal is an expression and encloses nothing at all.
> 
> Two rules ask this question of a tree walk that carries a verdict
> downwards, and both need enclosure rather than expression-hood:
> 
>   RM 7.4.1  "occurrences within derived type definitions or within
>              simple expressions are not allowed" -- the name of a
>              private type may stand as a type mark in the four
>              admitted declarations, so what the walk must know at
>              each step is whether it has passed inside a simple
>              expression;
>   RM 13.1   "A forcing occurrence is any occurrence other than in a
>              type or subtype declaration, ...  In any case, an
>              occurrence within an expression is always forcing" --
>              the exemptions are declarations and the taking-back is
>              positional, so the walk must know whether it has
>              passed inside an expression.
> 
> Were the class expression-hood instead, RM 13.1's exemption list
> would be empty of effect: every declaration it exempts names a type
> mark, a type mark is a name, and a name is an expression.
> 
> RM 7.4.1 says "simple expression" and RM 13.1 says "expression",
> and no Node_Kind tells the two apart -- the levels between them
> (RM 4.4's relation and expression) are operator applications, which
> are in the class under either reading.  So it is one class.

`ada83.c:2063`

### NODE_CLASS_PROGRAM_UNIT_DECLARATION = 1u << 2,

> RM 6, RM 7: the program units whose specification and body each
> open a declarative region carrying the unit's own name.  A body
> completes the declaration and denotes the same entity, so both
> carry the symbol that names the region.
> 
> A generic declaration is not one of them.  Its specification opens
> the region, and RM 12.1's generic formal part comes before that
> specification and inside the same declaration, where RM 8.3 leaves
> the unit's own name not yet visible.

`ada83.c:2106`

### NODE_CLASS_SUBPROGRAM_DECLARATION   = 1u << 3,

> RM 6.1, RM 6.3, RM 8.5: the declarations that declare a subprogram
> by writing a subprogram specification.  A generic instantiation may
> declare one too (RM 12.3), and only the symbol it created says
> whether it did, so it is not in the class.

`ada83.c:2117`

### NODE_CLASS_EXEMPT_FROM_FORCING      = 1u << 4,

> RM 13.1: "any occurrence other than in a type or subtype
> declaration, a subprogram specification, an entry declaration, a
> deferred constant declaration, a pragma, or a representation clause
> for the type itself".  These are the ones a node kind settles.  A
> deferred constant declaration is an object declaration and RM 7.4.3
> decides it from the object's own text; the representation clause is
> decided by which type is asking.  RM 9.1 makes a task specification
> that starts with `task type' a type declaration, so it is one of
> these too.

`ada83.c:2123`

### NODE_CLASS_TAKES_TYPE_FROM_CONTEXT  = 1u << 5

> RM 8.7: the expression forms that carry no type of their own until
> an interpretation is chosen -- a name (RM 4.1: an identifier or an
> expanded name alike), a call, an operator application -- together
> with the composite literals of RM 4.3 and RM 4.2 whose type simply
> is their context.  A numeric or character literal is deliberately
> absent: RM 2.4 gives an integer literal universal_integer and RM
> 4.2 gives a character literal a character type, and those are
> answers rather than questions.

`ada83.c:2134`

### typedef struct Node_Kind_Properties

> The syntax as data.  Syntax_Tree_Shape above says where a node's
> children are; this says what a node of each kind is.
> 
> Four of the columns are field offsets, on the same footing as
> Syntax_Tree_Shape's: a question of the form "which field of a node of
> this kind holds X" is answered by naming the field once per kind
> rather than by a switch reaching into a different arm of the union in
> each of its cases.  Offset zero means the kind has no such field --
> offset zero is Syntax_Node's KIND, which is never one of them.

`ada83.c:2145`

### typedef enum

> ---- The lowered form ----
> 
> Resolution's conclusions, in the shape code generation consumes
> without asking the syntax tree again.  Seven records carry the phase
> (see the table of contents); this table is the part of it that lives
> on a node, one row per field, on the same footing as
> Syntax_Tree_Shape's offsets and Node_Kind_Property_Table's.
> 
> Each row names the one Node_Kind that carries the lowering, where
> the field is, how wide it is, and what it holds until something
> fills it.  Two properties follow from the rows being in one place,
> and neither held while they were scattered over the union's arms:
> 
> - a FILL POINT can be total.  A function that fills a lowering
>   attaches it on every path it can leave by, and then UNFILLED at
>   the reader means one thing only — resolution never reached this
>   node — so the reader can report that rather than guess around it.
>   Fill_Aggregate_Descriptor is the model.
> 
> - a CLONE cannot inherit a conclusion.  Clone_Subtree exists to take
>   an unresolved tree out of a resolved one, so nothing resolution
>   decided may travel with it.  Discarding the lowered form from the
>   table is what keeps that true of a lowering added later: one that
>   is not listed does not compile.

`ada83.c:2172`

> True when NODE is of the kind that carries LOWERING and something

### Node_Identifier_List_Part

```c
Node_List *Node_Identifier_List_Part (Syntax_Node *node)
```

> RM 6.1, RM 9.5, RM 12.1, RM 3.7.1: the constructs written with a list
> of such specifications, and the list each is written with — a formal
> part for a subprogram specification and for the formal part of an
> accept statement, an entry declaration; a discriminant part for a
> generic formal type.  Every identifier one of these lists declares
> occurs immediately within a single declarative region (RM 8.1): the
> one associated with the construct that carries the list.
> 
> A generic formal subprogram is not among them: RM 12.1.3 gives it a
> subprogram specification, which is the first case.  Neither is a type
> declaration: its discriminant part is only half of what its region
> declares, and Check_Type_Declaration_Identifiers_Are_Distinct states
> the rule over the whole of it.

`ada83.c:8482`

### Identifier_List_Part_Repeats

```c
bool Identifier_List_Part_Repeats (Node_List *part,
```

> RM 8.3: "Two declarations that occur immediately within the same
> declarative region must not be homographs", and none of the entities
> an identifier list declares — formal parameter, discriminant — is
> overloadable, so equal identifiers are homographs outright and no
> parameter and result type profile enters into it.
> 
> True when the identifier at this position of the part repeats one that
> an earlier position of the same part already declares.  It is the
> later declaration that is illegal, and the one a caller installing
> symbols must leave undeclared, so that the region holds exactly one
> declaration of the identifier and RM 8.3 has nothing further to say
> about it.

> RM 9.5: an entry call statement is a statement that calls an entry.
> The callee may be written as a selected component naming an entry of
> another task, as the simple name of one of the enclosing task's own
> entries, or as either of those applied to arguments or to a family
> index — in every case it is the callee's symbol, or the resolution
> the call settled on, that says whether an entry was called.

### #define LOWERING_LIST(X)                                                    \

> Every lowering, once: the node kind that carries it, the field, and

> field's UNFILLED is written in four bytes — (uint32_t) -1, not -1 —
> because the row stores bits and the widths must agree; the third
> assertion below is what says so if it is written the other way.

### typedef struct

> A parse position that can be returned to.  The parser's whole reading
> state is the token in hand, the token behind it and the lexer, so a mark
> is those three; restoring one puts the parser back where it stood.  Used
> only where the grammar cannot be told apart on a single token of
> lookahead.

> the item list belongs to decides which legality rule it is held to.

### Parse_Simple_Expression

```c
Syntax_Node *Parse_Simple_Expression (Parser *p)
```

> RM 4.4: simple_expression is the level of the expression grammar
> below the relational operators and the logical ones, so parsing it is
> the precedence climb stopped one level short of a full expression.
> Parenthesising is what admits an operator of a lower level, and a
> parenthesised expression is a primary.

`ada83.c:9276`

> RM 3.7.3: choice ::= simple_expression | discrete_range | others
> | component_simple_name.  A choice is a SIMPLE expression: a
> relational or a logical operator at its top level is outside the
> production, and the parser refusing to read one is the whole of that
> rule.

`ada83.c:9285`

### —

> An item of an association list is either a positional expression or a
> choice list with its expression, and the two productions share their
> beginning: both open with a simple expression.  So one is read, and
> what follows it says which production was being read - an operator
> below simple_expression's level can only continue an expression, and
> `|`, `=>`, `..` and `range` can only continue a choice.

`ada83.c:9300`

### Parse_Association_List

```c
void Parse_Association_List (Parser *p, Node_List *list)
```

> Every parenthesised list Ada 83 writes is `( item {, item} )`: an
> actual parameter part (RM 6.4), an index constraint (RM 3.6.1), a
> discriminant constraint (RM 3.7.2), an aggregate (RM 4.3), a generic
> actual part (RM 12.3), a pragma's arguments (RM 2.8).  Not one of
> them has an empty alternative, so `()` closes a list that was never
> opened on any production.

`ada83.c:9306`

### Parse_Unary

```c
Syntax_Node *Parse_Unary (Parser *p, Precedence min_prec)
```

> RM 4.4 puts each prefix operator in exactly one production, and MIN_PREC
> says which production is being read:
> 
>   simple_expression ::= [unary_adding_operator] term {…}
>   term              ::= factor {multiplying_operator factor}
>   factor            ::= primary [** primary] | abs primary | not primary
> 
> So "+" and "-" may only open a simple expression, "abs" and "not" may
> only open a factor, and a primary opens nothing.  The operand each
> takes is named by the same three lines: a term for the unary adding
> operators, a primary for "abs" and "not" — which is why `- -J`,
> `ABS -J`, `NOT NOT B` and `K * -J` are none of them expressions.

`ada83.c:9345`

### Token_Kind connective    = TK_EOF;

> RM 4.4 writes the two outermost productions as closed lists:
> 
>   expression ::= relation {and relation} | relation {and then relation}
>                | relation {or  relation} | relation {or else relation}
>                | relation {xor relation}
>   relation   ::= simple_expression [relational_operator simple_expression]
>                | simple_expression [not] in range | … in type_mark
> 
> An expression therefore repeats ONE connective — mixing them needs
> parentheses — and a relation admits AT MOST ONE relational operator,
> which is what makes `0 < X < 101` no expression at all.  RM 4.4's
> factor is the same shape once more: "factor ::= primary [** primary]"
> admits at most one "**".
> 
> All three are properties of THIS level.  The right operand of every
> operator is read by a nested call at a higher precedence, so a
> second operator of the same rank arriving here is a repeat of the
> one before it, not a new production.

`ada83.c:9397`

### Precedence next_prec =

> RM 4.4: "factor ::= primary [** primary]" - a primary on each side
> of "**", so exponentiation associates neither way and the operand
> it reads is a primary.  Reading it at PREC_PRIMARY says both
> halves at once: no prefix operator opens a primary, and no infix
> operator continues one.  Every other operator climbs one level,
> which is what makes it group to the left (RM 4.5(6)).

`ada83.c:9478`

> RM 5.1 gives a statement its labels, each written `<<name>>` and
> any number of them.  RM 5.5 and RM 5.6 give a loop statement and a

### Parse_Body_Statement_Sequence

```c
void Parse_Body_Statement_Sequence (Parser *p, Node_List *list)
```

> The statement sequence of a body (subprogram, package, task, block),
> which owns its closing END.  After an error inside a nested compound
> statement, recovery can leave that statement's END IF / END LOOP /
> END CASE / END SELECT unconsumed; the plain sequence parser would stop
> there and the body would mistake it for its own END.  Swallow such
> orphans and resume, so one mangled statement cannot unravel the
> bracketing of everything around it.


> the first index says which.  An unconstrained array definition

### Parse_Component_List

```c
void Parse_Component_List (Parser *p, Node_List *components,
```

> RM 3.7's component_list, in all three of the forms it has:
> 
>     component_list ::= component_declaration {component_declaration}
>                      | {component_declaration} variant_part
>                      | null;
> 
> A record type definition has exactly one and so does every variant,
> which is why both are parsed here rather than each spelling out the
> production for itself.  None of the three forms is empty: `null;' is
> how Ada writes a component list with no components, and it is an
> alternative to the other two rather than a declaration that may
> stand beside them.  A list that is empty, or that writes `null'
> alongside something else, is therefore not a component list at
> all.

`ada83.c:10401`

> is no set of choices for RM 3.7.3's coverage rule to be about.

### Parse_Generic_Declaration

```c
Syntax_Node *Parse_Generic_Declaration (Parser *p)
```

> RM 12.1: generic_specification ::=
>      generic_formal_part subprogram_specification
>    | generic_formal_part package_specification
> RM 12.1 also requires that "the designator of a generic subprogram must

> follows a generic formal part, so the operator symbol form of RM 6.1 is

### static const struct Simple_Declaration_Form

> RM 3.1: these forms of basic declaration are each read whole by one
> parser and closed by the semicolon that ends every declaration, so the
> leading token, the parser and nothing else tell them apart.  The
> identifier row covers the object, number, exception and deferred
> constant declarations together with the object and exception renamings,
> all of which begin with an identifier list.  The three keywords that are
> NOT here — PROCEDURE, FUNCTION, PACKAGE and TASK — each open several
> distinct declarations that are told apart only further in.

### Resolve_Operand

```c
void Resolve_Operand (Syntax_Node *o, Type_Info *opnd_typ)
```

> THE context-fixing operation — the top-down half of RM 8.7.  Once a
> context type is known, every operand shape lands here:
> 
>   operators & names   select among their collected interpretations,
>   committed calls     re-resolve under the context they missed,
>   expanded literals   likewise,
>   character literals  bind to the context's enumeration,
>   everything unTyped  resolves with the context as its seed.
> 
> No caller needs a private retry protocol.

`ada83.c:11324`

```c

```

> RM 4.1.1 and RM 6.4 give an indexed component and a function
> call the same written form, so which of the two an application
> is belongs to resolution and must yield to the context on the
> same terms as the choice among callables (RM 8.7): a committed
> indexing whose type the context does not cover is reconsidered
> exactly as a committed call is.

`ada83.c:11348`

### Resolve_Operand

```c
Type_Info *base = Type_Base (opnd_typ);
```

> RM 4.3.2: a positional aggregate takes its bounds from the
> index range of its own applicable index constraint, so the
> type it is resolved against is the unconstrained one.  That
> anonymous base is built once per array type and kept on the
> type, so every aggregate of that type resolves to one entity.

`ada83.c:11390`

### typedef enum

> Which arm of Type_Info's class union a kind makes live.  Exactly one
> arm is live for any type, and reading through another is undefined
> behaviour rather than a stale answer, so the mapping is a total
> function of the kind and is stated once, in Type_Kind_Property_Table.
> A kind that keeps its whole description outside the union — integer,
> modular, task, incomplete, universal — selects TYPE_ARM_NONE.
> 
> Kind and arm are not the same axis.  Array and string share the
> array arm; record, private and limited private share the record arm;
> boolean, character and enumeration share the enumeration arm.  Any
> predicate that means "may I read this arm" is asking for the arm,
> not for the kind.

```c

```

> Two different questions are asked of RM 3.3.2's constraint forms,
> they have two different answers, and each therefore has its own
> function.
> 
> Type_Admitted_Constraint_Forms is RM 3.3.2's legality question:
> which forms may be written after a given type mark.  RM 3.8 settles
> the access case -- "the only forms of constraint that are allowed
> after the name of an access type in a subtype indication are index
> constraints and discriminant constraints" -- and RM 7.4.2 shows a
> private view's discriminants and hides everything else.  RM 3.3.2
> also withdraws a form once the mark already imposes it: "if an index
> constraint appears after a type mark in a subtype indication, the
> type mark must not already impose an index constraint."
> 
> Type_Constraint_Form asks RM 3.6.1 and RM 3.7.2's question instead:
> which form, if any, an object of the type still needs before its
> size and its discriminants are settled.  A constrained array admits
> no further index constraint and still answers INDEX here, because
> this question is about the class of the type rather than about what
> may follow the mark.
> 
> Constraint_Node_Form is neither: it reads the form off the
> constraint as written, from Node_Kind_Property_Table, and is exact
> only after Retag_Positional_Discriminant_Constraint has settled the
> parser's one ambiguity.

> RM 13.1: a representation clause fixes one aspect of a type's

> aspects nameable by a type representation clause are the three
> length-clause attributes of RM 13.2 -- SIZE, STORAGE_SIZE and SMALL --
> together with the enumeration codes of RM 13.3 and the record layout,
> alignment included, of RM 13.4.  A *set* of aspects, which
> is what a type accumulates as its declarative part is elaborated, is
> a bit set over this enumeration built with Representation_Aspect_Bit;
> keeping the two apart is what stops an aspect from being confused
> with a union of aspects.

### const Type_Kind_Properties Type_Kind_Property_Table[TYPE_COUNT] =

> RM 3.3, RM 3.5, RM 3.6-3.8, RM 7.4, RM 9.1: the type lattice as
> data.  Both questions a Type_Kind answers — which classes of the
> language the type belongs to, and which arm of the class union its
> Type_Info makes live — are read from this one table.  Nothing else
> in the compiler enumerates Type_Kind for either purpose.
> 
> A row naming no class describes something that is not a type: an
> unresolved name, a subprogram, a package.  TYPE_INCOMPLETE is in the
> same position for a different reason — RM 3.8.1 leaves the class of
> an incomplete type unknown until its full declaration, so the honest
> answer is the empty set rather than a guess.
> 
> That an incomplete type has no class and still makes an arm live is
> the clearest evidence that class and arm are two axes: RM 3.8.1 lets
> an incomplete declaration carry a discriminant part, those
> discriminants are held as record components, and they must survive
> until the completion claims them.
> 
> The array arm serves both array and string; the record arm serves
> record, both private kinds and incomplete, because RM 3.3 gives a
> private type discriminants and they are held as record components;
> the enumeration arm serves boolean and character as well as
> enumeration, because RM 3.5.2 makes those predefined enumeration
> types.

### —

> RM 7.4.4 names four sources of limitedness: "A private type
> declaration that includes the reserved word limited declares a
> limited type.  A task type is a limited type.  A type derived from a
> limited type is itself a limited type.  Finally, a composite type is
> limited if the type of any of its subcomponents is limited."
> 
> Only the first is answered by a declaration on its own.  The other
> three are answered by the type's structure, and how much of that
> structure can be seen depends on which view is in force where the
> question is asked (RM 7.4.2): under the partial view a private type
> is nothing but what its declaration said, so the walk stops there.
> That makes limitedness a property of the pair (type, point of
> compilation), and the walk carries the point with it — which is why
> an array of a limited private type is limited outside the declaring
> package and not limited inside it after the full type declaration
> has said the component is an integer.
> 
> The third and fourth clauses carry one more restriction.  RM 3.4
> derives a type's characteristics from its parent as the parent stood
> where the derivation was written, and RM 7.4.2 declares the
> operations a composite gets from a private component's full type "at
> the earliest place within the immediate scope of the composite type
> and after the full type declaration".  Both say the same thing: a
> type built out of a private type is limited at every point outside
> its own immediate scope, even a point where the constituent's full
> view is itself in force.  That is what MINIMUM_CONSTITUENT_VIEW
> carries down the walk: once some enclosing type is out of scope it is
> TYPE_VIEW_PARTIAL, and from there a private constituent answers from
> its declaration whatever else is visible here.
> 
> An access type has no subcomponents to be limited: RM 3.8 makes the
> designated object reachable through the value, not a part of it.  It
> is still limited when it was derived from a limited type, which is
> why the third clause is asked before that one.  The depth cap merely
> bounds the walk on a malformed lattice; RM 3.3 already forbids
> composite recursion that does not pass through an access type.

`ada83.c:11845`

### Narrowed_Constituent_View

```c
static Type_View_Kind Narrowed_Constituent_View (const Type_Info *t,
```

> RM 3.4 derives a type's characteristics from its parent as the parent
> stood where the derivation was written, and RM 7.4.2 declares the
> operations a composite gets from a private component's full type "at
> the earliest place within the immediate scope of the composite type
> and after the full type declaration".  Both say the same thing about
> a walk that has just reached T from outside T's own immediate scope:
> from here on nothing below T can be seen more fully than its own
> declaration showed.  An anonymous type has no immediate scope of its
> own to be outside of, so it narrows nothing; it is reached only
> through the named type that has already answered.

> Nor can the narrowing be applied while a generic instance is being
> elaborated: the scope in force there is the *template's*, because the
> template's own text is what is being re-resolved, so "outside this
> type's own package" would be answered about the wrong point in the
> program.  Crossing to the point of instantiation instead was tried
> and refuted — see this region's NOTES.md.

### Full_Characteristics_To_Depth

```c
static bool Full_Characteristics_To_Depth (const Type_Info *t,
```

> RM 7.4.2 divides the operations of a type in two.  "The operations
> that are implicitly declared by a private type declaration include
> basic operations … assignment …, membership tests, selected
> components for the selection of any discriminant, qualification, and
> explicit conversions", plus T'BASE, T'SIZE, A'CONSTRAINED, A'SIZE and
> A'ADDRESS, plus equality unless the declaration says limited.  Those
> exist wherever the type does.  Every other operation belongs to the
> other half:
> 
> > Within the package that declares the private type, the additional
> > operations implicitly declared by the full type declaration are
> > also available.
> 
> and, for a composite type built out of one,
> 
> > If a composite type has subcomponents of a private type and is
> > declared outside the package that declares the private type, then
> > the operations that are implicitly declared by the declaration of
> > the composite type include all operations that only depend on the
> > characteristics that result from the private type declaration
> > alone.  (For example the operator < is not included for a
> > one-dimensional array type.)  If the composite type is itself
> > declared within the package that declares the private type … these
> > additional operations are implicitly declared at the earliest place
> > within the immediate scope of the composite type and after the full
> > type declaration.
> 
> So the question "does this operation exist here" is the question
> "are the characteristics this operation reads the full ones, here" —
> the same walk as Type_Is_Limited, carrying the same point of
> compilation and narrowing at the same places, with a different
> question at the leaves and one parameter, because RM 7.4.2's
> "characteristics" reach exactly as far as the operation asking does.
> CHARACTERISTICS_REACH_KIND is that distance, and the three values are
> three sentences of the RM; `b74205a` and `b74205b` are what separate
> them, in one file each and in both directions.

### Safe_Number_Model_Of

```c

```

> RM 3.5.8 attaches every safe-number attribute to "the base type of
> T", so the model these formulas read is the base type's and not the
> subtype's — T'SAFE_LARGE is stated in terms of T'BASE'MANTISSA, and
> T'SAFE_LARGE = T'BASE'SAFE_LARGE only because of that.
> 
> RM 3.5.7: the safe numbers have the same mantissa length B as the
> model numbers and an exponent range -E .. +E, with E
> implementation-defined and at least the 4*B of the model numbers.
> E is chosen here as the largest value for which every safe number is
> a normalised number of the backing format: the smallest positive
> safe number is 2.0**(-E-1), so E = -MACHINE_EMIN makes it exactly
> the format's smallest normalised number.  RM 3.5.10 gives fixed
> point no exponent of its own — there the safe numbers of T are
> simply the model numbers of T'BASE.

`ada83.c:12154`

### Real_Model_Smallest

```c
double Real_Model_Smallest (Real_Model model)
```

> RM 3.5.8's own formulas for the model numbers of a floating point
> type, and RM 3.5.10's for a fixed point type:
> 
>   T'SMALL   = 2.0**(-T'EMAX - 1)
>   T'LARGE   = 2.0**T'EMAX * (1.0 - 2.0**(-T'MANTISSA))
>   T'EPSILON = 2.0**(1 - T'MANTISSA)
>   T'LARGE   = (2**T'MANTISSA - 1) * T'SMALL        (fixed point)
> 
> The same three formulas answer the safe numbers when they are given

### Subtype_Is_Constrained_To_Depth

```c
static bool Subtype_Is_Constrained_To_Depth (const Type_Info *type_info,
```

> RM 3.6.1 / RM 3.7.2 / RM 3.8: does a constraint apply to this
> subtype?  RM 12.3.2, RM 12.3.4 and RM 12.3.5 each ask exactly this
> of an actual subtype, of an array's component subtype, and of an
> access type's designated subtype, so it is asked here once.
> 
> The answer is total.  An array subtype is constrained by an index
> constraint and a subtype of a type with discriminants by a
> discriminant constraint; RM 3.8 makes a constraint on an access
> subtype apply to the objects it designates, so an access subtype is
> constrained exactly when its designated subtype is.  A subtype of
> any other class — scalar, task, a record type with no discriminants
> — has nothing further to constrain and so is constrained already.
> That is why the matching rules may exempt scalar types without
> changing any answer, and why this predicate needs no exemption.
> 
> The depth cap bounds the walk on a lattice where two incomplete
> access types complete each other; no constraint form is allowed on
> an access subtype whose designated type is itself an access type,
> so a well-formed lattice never descends more than once.

### typedef enum

> RM 3.2, RM 6.1, RM 8.3, RM 9.5, RM 10.1: the classes of declared
> entity, as a set of Symbol_Kind.  The seven primitive classes are the
> RM's own; the derived classes are unions of them, so a rule stated
> over "the subprograms" and a rule stated over "what may be a library
> unit" cannot drift apart.  A kind in no class describes something the
> questions below do not reach: a type, a subtype, an exception, the
> name of a statement.

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
> The rest of §12, declared.  Everything the semantic phase can say has
> an entry here: name resolution, type checking, folding, and the
> legality pass that runs over the settled tree.  A function defined in
> the body and missing from this table is invisible to a reader who
> comes to the specification to find out what the phase is able to do,
> which is the one thing a specification is for.
> 
> The order is the body's order and the headings are the body's own, so
> a name found here is found there.  A few of §12's functions are
> absent still: their profiles name a type the rule they belong to
> declares beside itself, and a declaration cannot precede its own
> vocabulary.  NOTES.md lists them with the type each waits on.

```c

```

> The symbol whose parameter profile a call's actuals are measured
> against.  RM 8.5: a subprogram renaming declares its own formal
> names, so named association uses the renaming, but the profile it
> repeats is the renamed declaration's and the formal subtypes come
> from there.  Where the two cannot be told apart — anything that is
> not a subprogram renaming repeating a conforming profile — the
> entity called is its own profile.

`ada83.c:3648`

### typedef enum

> Legality is a traversal of its own, over the tree resolution left
> behind, and it hosts the rules of the language that cannot be
> decided until one interpretation of the whole expression has been
> chosen (RM 8.7).
> 
> Resolution cannot host them.  It reaches a construct more than once:
> an outer context that rejects an inner reading already committed to
> sends the binder round again, and a diagnostic written on the way to
> a reading later discarded cannot be withdrawn, because diagnostics
> are written out as they are reported and nothing accumulates them.
> 
> The traversal therefore runs once every compilation unit in the
> compilation has been resolved, and before the error count decides
> whether code generation happens.  It may assume what resolution
> guarantees: the interpretation is recorded on the node — SYMBOL,
> TYPE, and for an application APPLY.RESOLUTION — every expression
> node that has a type has its final one, and nothing will revisit the
> node afterwards.  It visits every node of a unit exactly once and
> dispatches on the node's kind; that dispatch is where a legality
> rule belongs, rather than in the resolver.
> 
> Three things a rule may need are not on the node, because they are
> about where the node stands, so the traversal carries them.
> 
> The first is the position a name occupies.  RM 12.3's generic_name is
> the one position in the language that admits a name denoting a
> generic unit; RM 10.1.1's context clause and RM 2.8's pragmas name
> compilation units rather than denoting entities, and are not name
> positions at all.

`ada83.c:3657`

### typedef struct Enclosing_Unit

> The second is the chain of program units the node is inside,
> innermost first.  RM 12.1's rule about a generic unit's name opens
> with "Outside the specification and body of a generic unit", so being
> inside one is the rule's own antecedent rather than an exception
> bolted onto it.

### Check_Aggregate_Type_Is_Determined

```c

```

> RM 4.3: "The type of an aggregate must be determinable solely from
> the context in which the aggregate appears, excluding the aggregate
> itself, but using the fact that this type must be composite and not
> limited."
> 
> MUST be determinable.  When the context is an overloaded name and two
> of the readings that survive it would give an aggregate actual two
> different types, nothing in the language chooses between them, and
> the program is illegal rather than resolved by preference.  The RM's
> own note says why no tie-break is available: "the determination of
> the type of an aggregate cannot use any information from within the
> aggregate.  In particular, this determination cannot use the type of
> the expression of a component association, or the form or the type of
> a choice."  So the number of dimensions, the number of associations,
> the completeness of the aggregate and the length it implies are all
> silent, and RM 4.3.2 adds that the restrictions on where an others
> choice may appear are silent too.
> 
> This is asked here because here is where the surviving readings of a
> name are held — the rule is about the aggregate, so it is reported at
> the aggregate, but it cannot be answered from one.  A reading another
> hides (RM 8.3) was never a competing reading and is passed over.

> RM 4.1.3 gives a selected component six readings, and this is where
> the compiler decides which one is written:
> 
>   (a) a discriminant                (b) a record component
>   (c) a task entry                  (d) an explicit dereference, .ALL
>   (e) an entity in a package's visible part
>   (f) an entity declared immediately within a named enclosing
>       construct
> 
> (e) and (f) are the two expanded-name readings.  Whichever applies,
> the decision is recorded on the node — a component index for (a) and
> (b), a designated type for (d), the denoted symbol otherwise — so
> Generate_Selected has only to address what was decided here.
> 
> Each reading below answers "did the node land on its entity", not
> "what type did it land on": an expanded name can denote a procedure,
> which has no type at all.

### Resolve_Enclosing_Construct_Selector

```c
static bool Resolve_Enclosing_Construct_Selector (Syntax_Node *node)
```

> RM 4.1.3, on the precedence of the expanded-name reading:
> 
>   "If, according to the visibility rules, there is at least one
>    possible interpretation of the prefix of a selected component as
>    the name of an enclosing subprogram or accept statement, then the
>    only interpretations considered are those of rule (f), as expanded
>    names (no interpretations of the prefix as a function call are
>    then considered)."
> 
> So this reading is tried before the prefix is resolved as an
> expression — resolving it first is what would turn the name of an
> enclosing parameterless function into a call to it, and make `F.C`
> read as a component of F's result.
> 
> The scope walk answers "does a construct of this name enclose the
> reference"; it is not itself the region rule (f) asks about.  A block
> statement, a loop statement and an accept statement each push a scope
> that inherits the enclosing subprogram's owner, so the innermost scope
> owned by the named construct is usually not the construct's own
> declarative region.  RM 8.1 makes each of those a region of its own,
> and rule (f) admits only what is declared immediately within the
> construct itself — so the selector is looked up in the construct's own
> scope, and only among the declarations that occur there.  A function
> declared in an inner block does not hide the enumeration literal the
> expanded name denotes.


> RM 6.4: an actual parameter part is a sequence of associations, each

> so it is built here, once, for all of them.
> 
> COMMITTING marks the one build that belongs to this apply's own
> resolution: it resolves each actual on the way past and reports the
> illegalities it meets.  A speculative probe — "what else could this
> expression mean" — passes FALSE, reads the types the actuals already
> carry, and stays silent, so that a reading the resolver ends up
> rejecting cannot leave diagnostics behind.

> RM 4.3: an aggregate has no type of its own; its type comes from the
> context it lands in.  An aggregate actual therefore contributes no
> type here and so constrains no candidate — a NULL actual type is what
> Arguments_Match_Profile reads as "admits any formal".  The formal
> supplies the aggregate's type once the callee is settled.

> argument list: one for a call of a member of an entry family, since
> RM 9.5 writes the family index at the head of the same list, and
> zero everywhere else.

> This is the one fill point of LOWERING_FORMAL_ORDINAL and it is
> total — every association it walks leaves with an ordinal, the one
> whose written name names no formal included, and that is a different
> answer from never having been bound rather than the same one.  Code
> generation reads the stamp through Actual_Formal_Index and does not
> search a second time.  Context fixing is otherwise delegated whole to
> Resolve_Operand, which is THE top-down half of RM 8.7; a call keeps

> every library unit, and the declaration of a library unit is assumed
> to occur immediately within it.  By RM 8.3 the identifier of a
> library unit may therefore not be a homograph of one of STANDARD's
> own declarations — and two declarations of one identifier are
> homographs unless overloading is allowed for both.  Of the three
> forms a library unit can take (RM 10.1: subprogram, package,
> generic unit) only a subprogram is overloadable, so a library
> subprogram may share the name of the enumeration literals TRUE and

>   RM 4.1.2 make them parts of the object the prefix names;

>   dereference is the same thing, so an indexed or selected component
>   whose prefix is of an access type is a variable however that access

>   of a name is a function call, then the name denotes a component, a
>   slice, an attribute, an entry, or an entry family, either of the

> Everything else — a literal, an aggregate, a function call, an
> attribute, a qualified expression, an allocator, an expression with an
> operator — is either not a name at all or a name that denotes no
> object, so it is not the name of a variable.

### typedef struct

> RM 13.1 says a representation clause does not affect the semantics of
> a program.  The converse holds with as much force: what code
> generation emitted for a type is not part of the type.  The number of
> an LLVM global and the name of an LLVM function are facts about one
> compilation's output; the type is what the declaration declared.
> 
> Four such identifiers were fields of Type_Info, and while they were,
> a question about a type's meaning could be answered by asking whether
> a global had been written yet: Emit_Type_Byte_Size read a record's
> size from whether a descriptor had been emitted, an array aggregate
> decided from the same test whether to take its bounds from that
> descriptor instead of from its own, and Replicate_Component_Subtype
> had to zero the descriptor by hand after copying a type, because a
> whole-record copy carried an emitted global's number to a type it was
> not emitted for.  Here they are a memo table owned by §13, keyed by
> the type it was emitted for, and nothing upstream of code generation
> can name them.
> 
> The table's lifetime is the compilation's, because the artifacts' is:
> a global emitted once is referred to from every later use of the
> type.  That is the opposite of the bound cache below, whose lifetime
> is one function, because a register outlives nothing.  A memo is
> sound only where its key outlives its answer, and these two are the
> two ends of that rule.
> 
> Rows are allocated one at a time and the table holds their addresses,
> so a row's address is good for the whole compilation and growing the
> table cannot move an answer out from under a caller.

`ada83.c:4165`

### struct Bound_Cache_Entry

> RM 3.6.1 and RM 4.3.2 both evaluate a bound expression once per
> elaboration.  The register that holds the result belongs to the
> function that emitted it, not to the bound -- a Type_Bound reached
> through a Type_Info is shared by every use of that type -- so the
> answer is kept here, beside the emission it belongs to, and
> forgotten wholesale when emission moves to another function.

`ada83.c:4343`

### typedef enum

> RM 3.5.5 defines 'IMAGE, 'VALUE and 'WIDTH one family of scalar type
> at a time: a character literal is its own spelling, an enumeration
> literal is its identifier in upper case, a real value has a decimal
> image, and every other scalar has an integer image.  The three
> attributes are the same classification asked three times, so they
> ask it here and cannot disagree.

`ada83.c:5164`

### typedef struct Discrete_Value_Range

> RM 3.5: the range of a scalar type's base type, as integers.  A
> position range counts literals from zero, which is what 'VAL's
> argument is; a value range is the representation, which is what
> 'SUCC, 'PRED and the number a 'VALUE image denotes are.  For an
> enumeration type with a RM 13.3 representation clause the two
> differ, so they are separate questions with separate answers.

`ada83.c:5184`

### Emit_Implicit_Initial_Value

```c
void Emit_Implicit_Initial_Value (uint32_t   address,
```

> RM 3.2.1: the implicit initial values an object takes when nothing
> initializes it explicitly — null for an access object and for every
> access subcomponent, the declared default for every record
> component, and the same rules again for each element of an array.
> RM 4.8 gives an object created by an allocator exactly these
> ("Initializations are then performed as for a declared object"), so
> the object is named by an address and measured by registers: a frame
> slot, a collection block, and an array whose bounds are known only
> at run time all reach the one rule the same way.
> 
> ELEMENT_COUNT and BYTE_EXTENT are i64 registers; zero means "none",
> since no emitted value occupies register zero.

`ada83.c:5231`

### typedef struct

> One dimension of an array aggregate as resolution determined it.
> LOW and HIGH are the bounds the aggregate itself has — from the
> smallest and largest choice when it is named, from the lower bound
> plus the component count when it is positional (RM 4.3.2).  The
> constraint those bounds must satisfy is not copied here; it stays
> on the type, reached through Array_Dimension_Effective_Bound.

`ada83.c:5777`

### bool       low_from_choices;

> RM 4.3.2 gives an aggregate with named associations bounds of its
> own — "the smallest and largest choices given" — where a
> positional aggregate and one with an others choice take theirs
> from the applicable index constraint.  Emission has to know which,
> because a subtype whose bounds live in a runtime descriptor
> evaluated the second kind once at elaboration and must be read
> rather than re-evaluated, while the first kind belongs to the
> choices and is not in that descriptor at all.

`ada83.c:5788`

### uint32_t   positional_count;

> When HIGH_FROM_POSITIONAL_COUNT, the number of components the
> upper bound is derived from: RM 4.3.2 puts it at the lower bound
> plus the count less one, which is only foldable when the lower
> bound folds.

`ada83.c:5799`

### typedef struct

> A component association with its choice already classified and its
> endpoints already folded where they fold.  Positional items and
> named choices reach emission in the same shape, and a multi-choice
> list arrives already flattened: one entry per choice.

`ada83.c:5813`

### typedef struct Aggregate_Descriptor

> Everything code generation needs to know about an array aggregate
> that is a property of the aggregate rather than of the point of
> use.  Emission reads it; it never re-walks the item list to
> rediscover a bound.

`ada83.c:5830`

### typedef enum

> RM 4.9: the ways an expression can fail to be static, each arm naming
> the sentence of RM 4.9 it falls outside.  A context that requires a
> static expression can then say which rule was broken and not only
> that one was.

`ada83.c:5868`

### typedef struct

> A storage locus names a readable/writable interval of bits: a
> byte-aligned address, a displacement below one storage unit, and a
> width.  Record components and array elements both resolve to loci;
> exactly one load and one store consume them (REPRESENTATION.md).

`ada83.c:6017`

### typedef enum

> Where an assignment puts its value.  The choice between a
> representation store, a bit-window store, a packed element store and
> a byte copy is a property of the target's type and layout, not of
> the statement that writes it, so a destination is built by a
> constructor and consumed by one store.

`ada83.c:6034`

### typedef struct

> One formal's slot in a call.  The subprogram path and the entry
> path both fill this: what the slot passes, how that value is
> spelled at the call site, and — for a formal copied in and out —
> where its final value must be written back to.  A zero register is
> "none": temporaries are numbered from one.

`ada83.c:6085`

### #define TASKING_BYTES(first, count) \

> ==== The tasking records (RM 9) ==================================
> 
> The tasking runtime keeps all of its state in four shapes: a task
> control block per task object (RM 9.1), a rendezvous record per
> entry call (RM 9.5), a master record per master (RM 9.4), and a
> two-word list node that links tasks to their master and masters to
> their owner.
> 
> Two authors address these records.  One is the LLVM the runtime
> prelude is written in, emitted verbatim by the Emit_Runtime_*
> phases.  The other is the expander, which reaches into the same
> records for accept, select, abort, a task body's own activation and
> completion, and the task attributes of RM 9.9.  Both splice their
> offsets from the macros below, so a field cannot mean one thing in
> the runtime and another in generated code.
> 
> Every reference is byte-scaled — getelementptr i8, ptr <base>,
> i64 <offset> — so that moving a field is one edit here and nothing
> anywhere else.
> 
> The layout assumes an eight-byte pointer and a thread identifier
> that fits in one; the assertion on POINTER_ALLOC_SIZE below records
> that dependence rather than leaving it to be discovered.
> 
> Each record also names the bytes no field occupies.  The assertion
> for a record compares the union of its fields against its size
> minus its unused bytes, so a field that moves onto another, a hole
> that opens, and a size that no longer matches all fail the build
> instead of miscompiling a task.

`ada83.c:6255`

> field, width in bytes.
> 
> BODY_FUNCTION and PARENT_FRAME are the task body and the frame it
> closes over; THREAD_IDENTIFIER is null until the task is activated
> (RM 9.3).  COMPLETED and TERMINATED are the two states of RM 9.4,
> and ABORT_PENDING is the abnormality of RM 9.10.  MASTER_RECORD is
> the master this task depends on and OWNED_MASTER_RECORDS the
> masters it is itself; AWAITING_TERMINATE_ALTERNATIVE and PASSIVE
> drive the termination consensus of RM 9.4.  The remaining four are

> ═══ RM 4.9: static expressions and static subtypes ════════════════
> "An expression of a scalar type is said to be static if and only if
> every primary is one of those listed in (a) through (h) below, every
> operator denotes a predefined operator, and the evaluation of the
> expression delivers a value (that is, it does not raise an
> exception)."
> 
> The arms below are the RM's own, in the RM's order.  The last clause
> of the sentence — that evaluation delivers a value — is a property of
> the value and is not decided here: an expression this answers
> STATICNESS_STATIC for may still fail it.

> RM 4.9: "A static subtype is either a scalar base type, other than a

> 
> "Imposing on a static subtype" makes the question one about the whole
> chain of subtypes and not about the outermost alone: a static range
> imposed on a nonstatic subtype yields a nonstatic subtype.  The same
> walk carries "other than a generic formal type" to a type derived

> distinguishes the two.

### unsigned long long Value_Magnitude_Limit (void)

> RM 2.4 and RM 3.5.5: the magnitude of a literal is accumulated
> unsigned and at twice the width of the arithmetic type, and is

> arithmetic type's first value — as soon as it passes.  A saturating
> accumulator needs no branch, so the scan keeps its shape, and the
> single test at the return catches every literal that denotes no

> and (2**(n-1)+1)**2 still fits in 2n bits.

> Forty LLVM functions, one C emitter each, named for the runtime

> being believed.

### typedef enum

> An operand is whatever may stand in an instruction's operand
> position: a register a previous instruction produced, an integer or
> float literal the assembler spells inline, or the null pointer.
> Every operand carries the representation it is read at, so no
> instruction combinator has to be told the type a second time.
> 
> Admitting the literal as an operand is what removes the `add iN 0, K`
> that materialising a constant into a register otherwise costs, and
> what lets one combinator serve a call site whose operand is static
> and a call site whose operand is only known at run time — the two
> cases that today are spelled as separate functions, or as one
> function with a static value, a register and a discriminating
> boolean.

> The spelling of an operand, and the `<type> <spelling>` pair.  The
> buffer is a compound literal with the caller's block scope, so two
> operands may appear in one Emit call without sharing storage.  Neither
> macro emits anything, so both are safe as sibling arguments.

`ada83.c:4410`

> than a register; a fold whose terms are all in one block should use

### Check_Kind_Bit

```c
uint32_t Check_Kind_Bit (Check_Kind kind)
```

> ===================== §13.2 The check algebra =======================
> 
>   A runtime check is three things and no more:
> 
> a CONDITION under which the program is wrong,
> the EXCEPTION RM 11.1 says to raise when it is,
> the CLASS RM 11.7 lets a pragma turn off.
> 
>   Check_Predicate carries the first, Exception_Kind the second,
>   Check_Permission the third together with the answer for this entity.
>   Emit_Runtime_Check is the only emitter of a classified check, and
>   Check_Permission_For is the only place the compiler asks whether a
>   pragma reaches one.
> 
>   Two erasures must not be confused.  A check RM 11.7 permits omitting
>   is erased on the programmer's authority, and RM 11.7(3) makes the
>   execution erroneous if the situation it guarded against then arises.
>   A check proved redundant is erased on the compiler's own authority
>   and the program keeps its meaning exactly.  Only the second kind may
>   be applied without a pragma; only the first excuses the compiler from
>   being right.  The elimination laws below are all of the second kind.

`ada83.c:32169`

### uint32_t Unit_Suppressed_Checks;

> RM 11.7(6): a pragma SUPPRESS naming an entity gives the permission
> for that entity; without a name it gives the permission throughout the
> enclosing declarative region, and for a compilation unit throughout
> the unit.  The nameless form is recorded on the region's owning
> symbol - the subprogram, package or task the region belongs to - or,
> at library level, in Unit_Suppressed_Checks.

`ada83.c:32222`

### Symbol *region = cg ? cg->current_function : NULL;

> The region-wide permission reaches every check emitted inside the
> region, including those in nested bodies, so the walk climbs the
> chain of defining scopes rather than stopping at the innermost.
> The hop bound guards against a malformed scope cycle; it is not a
> limit on legal nesting depth.

`ada83.c:32240`

### Check_Join

```c
Check_Predicate Check_Join (Check_Predicate first, Check_Predicate second)
```

> Two checks of the same class raising the same exception, with nothing
> between them, are one check whose failure condition is the disjunction
> of theirs.  The join is a control-flow fusion only: both operands are
> already materialised i1 registers, so no evaluation is moved, added or
> removed.  What it removes is one conditional branch and the basic
> block that branch needed.
> 
> De Morgan does the negation for free whenever the two predicates agree
> in sense; only a mixed pair pays for a complement.

`ada83.c:32266`

> -------------------- The elimination laws --------------------------
> 
> A check may be erased when the compiler can prove it cannot fail.
> Every law below is stated over intervals whose endpoints are known at
> compile time, because that is what the front end knows exactly and
> LLVM does not: LLVM sees integers, the front end sees Ada subtypes.
> 
> The laws erase the branch and the raise.  They never erase the
> evaluation of the value being checked - that evaluation is part of the
> program, not part of the check.

`ada83.c:32318`

> and named numbers, and returns a NaN for everything else - so a
> bound that merely looks constant, such as one naming a variable
> or a function result, is not known here.

### Static_Endpoint_Compare

